beats.lead: Google did not build DeepDream to make trippy art
beats.text: It was built to catch the network's mistakes.
beats.note: In 2015, engineers needed a way to check whether a trained neural network had learned the right thing, not just the popular thing.

beats.text: Asked to picture a dumbbell, the network kept adding a muscular arm to lift it.
beats.note: Every training photo of a dumbbell happened to include the arm doing the lifting, so the network had never seen one alone.

beats.text: So the engineers flipped the idea. Instead of asking what a photo showed, they asked the network to exaggerate whatever it half recognised.
beats.note: Their own description: whatever you see there, I want more of it. Show it clouds, and a network trained on animals starts filling the sky with birds.

beats.name: Mordvintsev, Olah and Tyka
beats.role: The Google engineers who published the technique, naming it Inceptionism after the neural network it ran on, itself named after the film Inception.

beats.text: The code went public a month later. The name that stuck was DeepDream.

beats.line: It started as a bug report and ended as an art movement.
